newsitem.title: USA: Ahmanson bids $6.5 billion for Great Western.
newsitem.headline: Ahmanson bids $6.5 billion for Great Western.

text.p: H.F. Ahmanson & Co. Tuesday launched a $6.5 billion hostile takeover bid for rival thrift Great Western Financial Corp. in a deal that would combine the nation's two largest savings and loan companies.
The proposed merger would create a powerhouse with $93 billion in assets, $63.4 billion in deposits and 600 branches after about 200 overlapping offices are closed.
The proposed merger would also represent the latest step in the rapid consolidation of California's banking and thrift sector.
While Ahmanson said it would prefer a friendly merger with Great Western, the Los Angeles-based thrift already is girding itself for a hostile takeover should the offer be rejected.
"We're emphasizing our desire to have a negotiated transaction, but we're taking the usual legal steps to ensure our position," Ahmanson President Bruce Willison said in a telephone interview.

To strengthen its case, Ahmanson filed a lawsuit in Delaware Tuesday seeking to block Great Western's "poison pill." The thrift also hired proxy solicitation firm MacKenzie Partners Inc. and proposed to nominate three individuals to Great Western's board of directors.
"We believe that three individuals we've nominated can certainly make their voices known with regard to the worthiness of our transaction," Willison said.

Ahmanson, the nation's largest savings and loan, made the offer Monday night. Under terms of the proposed deal, Ahmanson would swap 1.05 of its shares for each Great Western share, an offer that would value the nation's second largest thrift at a premium of more than $24 over its closing price.
Based on Tuesday's closing price, the bid valued Great Western stock at $47.12 a share.

Great Western Financial President John Maher said his company was reviewing the offer and would respond when it had an opportunity to fully review and evaluate the proposal with its board of directors and advisers.
Great Western stock jumped $10.625 to $44.875 and Ahmanson added $4.375 to $44.875, both in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
Ahmanson said the merger would result in $400 million in savings a year, consolidation of about 25 percent of the branches in the combined system and an unspecified number of job cuts.
If completed, Ahmanson said it would incur a one-time restructuring charge of $400 million and may need to take additional provision for loan losses of up to $150 million.
Analysts said the company would probably need to cut thousands of jobs from its combined work force of about 23,000 employees to achieve the level of savings it is looking for.

Great Western, based in Chatsworth, Calif., has about 14,300 employees and 1,150 offices, mostly in California and Florida. Ahmanson, based in Irwindale, owns several savings banks, including two big thrifts in New York state, and has about 450 branch offices.
Ahmanson said the expected cost savings, along with stock repurchases, would boost its earnings per share this year and over the next two years.
It also said revenue growth of the combined company would exceed any revenue losses associated with the merger but made no assurances some revenues will not be lost.

Ahmanson has hired the law firm of Sullivan & Cromwell and investment bankers Credit Suisse First Boston and Montgomery Securities to advise it on the merger. This is the same team that Wells Fargo lined up for its protracted, yet successful, hostile $11 billion bid for First Interstate Bancorp, which was completed last April.

Willison said there had been "conceptual discussions" between the two thrifts about a year ago, but the talks failed to produce a deal. He said Ahmanson's unsolicited offer Monday evening was a way to get those talks going again.
"Sometimes you need to put a firm offer on the table to get discussions kick-started," Willison said.
"It was our sense that the overall strategic and financial rationales for this deal were so compelling that it encouraged us to move forward."
Ahmanson said the deal would be accounted for as a purchase, would be tax-free and was subject to approval by both companies' boards and regulators.

Despite Wall Street's favorable reaction to the proposed deal, several investors and takeover specialists speculated that Great Western would try to line up a "white knight" or that Ahmanson would have to raise its offer.
"This deal could take a long way to work itself out. A lot of things could happen, including involvement by another financial institution," said Steve Cohen, analyst with Kellner, DiLeo and Co.
Some takeover traders were betting Washington Mutual Savings Bank, which has expressed an interest to expand its California franchise, may emerge as a white knight.
However, officials with Washington Mutual said it has not had discussions with Great Western. "We're not aware of any contacts between the two companies," a spokesman for Washington Mutual said.

Ahmanson Chief Executive Officer Charles Rinehart shrugged off such speculation, saying he believed Washington Mutual was too busy consolidating its recent acquisition of Keystone Holdings Inc. and Keystone's primary subsidiary, American Savings Bank to launch a bid for Great Western.
Rinehart said he believes Ahmanson's offer was compelling as it stands. However, he did not rule out raising the bid.
"I think we have a compelling offer as it stands and the reaction of the market suggests that they do as well. So at this stage, its best for us to see what happens," he said.
Madeline Kleiner, senior executive vice president and general counsel for Ahmanson, said the company believes it is possible the merger could be consummated by the third quarter.
Other California thrifts, such as Glendale Federal Bank, rose in response to the news. Glendale's shares rose $1.88 to $27.50 a share.
